channel.title: Noticias del Mundo — Ciencia
channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: Hatching a plan to ensure Australia's native turtles survive and thrive
item.description: How a citizen science program is saving thousands of turtles even as researchers learn more about them. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Gavin McGrath

item.title: Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
item.description: EU warns COP31 risks turning into a 'fossil summit' as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
item.description: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Spots Drifting Twilight Clouds
item.description: Description NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured these drifting clouds on Oct. 31, 2026, the 5,061st Martian day, or sol, of the mission. The rover uses its navigation cameras to capture post-sunset clouds, called twilight clouds, which appear for only a short time each fall over Gale Crater, which it has been exploring for more than […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
item.description: Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
item.description: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
item.description: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
item.description: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
item.description: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Record-setting X-ray laser reliably generates flashes with wavelengths shorter than distances between atoms
item.description: Researchers from DESY and European XFEL have demonstrated reliable production and transport of X-ray laser flashes with a wavelength of about 0.04 nanometers (or a photon energy of 30,000 electronvolts) at European XFEL, raising their own world record. This means that the X-ray's wavelength is much shorter than typical distances between neighboring atoms in solids, which enables the study of materials with higher spatial resolution than before. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
item.description: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy. NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Abby Tabor

item.title: Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts
item.description: Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New hemp plant produces no detectable THC, potentially reducing risk of crop destruction
item.description: Scientists at Texas A&M AgriLife Research, a member of The Texas A&M University System, have developed a hemp plant that produces no detectable cannabinoids, including THC. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
item.description: "We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Tested on mushrooms, an AI model shows potential for detecting crop stress with far fewer computations
item.description: A new artificial intelligence (AI) model can detect stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique, allowing changes in crop health to be monitored over time. Developed by a team of researchers at Penn State, the new model shows promise for accurately detecting crop stress caused by drought, disease, nutrient deficiency and other causes while using less computing power than some existing AI methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can Instagram reduce prejudice? Study reveals the potential and limits of social media contact
item.description: A research team at the University of Potsdam has conducted a field experiment to investigate whether contact through social media can reduce prejudice. The findings suggest that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for just three days can lead to more favorable attitudes—not only toward the group represented by the profile. The study was published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a season without their 'admiral' showed the Rockets what they were missing
item.description: Fred VanVleet is commanding the surging Rockets after an ACL injury derailed his 2025-26 season. Fuente: ESPN.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Wright

item.title: Global analysis reveals how lakes amplify glacier ice loss
item.description: Glacial lakes can accelerate the retreat of glaciers. If glaciers border a lake, the water can melt the ice from underneath; furthermore, chunks of ice can break off and fall into the lake. The extent to which these processes influence the situation, compared with other factors, had not been sufficiently clarified at a global level until now. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure
item.description: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes
item.description: Mitochondria are essential components of the cells of most organisms, including humans. They are often referred to as the cell's powerhouses because they produce the energy needed for cellular functions. However, mitochondria originally evolved from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Amazon communities have a complicated relationship with giant anacondas; a 2025 study explores why some people fear them while others live alongside them
item.description: Communities in the Lower Amazon have a multifaceted relationship with giant anacondas, dealing with folklore and livestock concerns. The presence of these snakes is often rooted in local myths, but practical encounters create conflicts. Killing anacondas frequently stems from protecting domestic animals rather than pure fear. Researchers indicate that the people's perceptions of the snakes have altered due to economic considerations. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale
item.description: Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. As many viruses have not been grown in a lab, connecting them to their natural hosts has been difficult. A new bioinformatics toolkit and database are now available to help researchers make those associations at an unprecedented scale. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El Niño created a skiers' paradise in Chile—now it's Sierra Nevada and southern Rockies' turn
item.description: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier's dream, bringing lots of snow to California's Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño's supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Practical organ-on-a-chip platform helps assess the toxicity of environmental chemicals
item.description: Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New sources of neurotoxin linked to algal blooms uncovered in Florida and Kansas
item.description: Researchers have identified two previously unreported strains of freshwater cyanobacteria capable of producing a potent neurotoxin that poses risks to people, pets, wildlife and water resources and that some scientists suspect may have contributed to previous animal deaths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bumblebees challenge long-held beliefs about brain size and intelligence
item.description: Bigger brains mean greater intelligence, or so conventional wisdom goes. After all, humans have much larger brains than most other animals and are generally considered the planet's most intelligent species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Is it genuine love—or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
item.description: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation—these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don't want to let that person out of your sight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Witnessing generosity from low-income donors more likely to elicit giving from observers, research finds
item.description: Billionaire Warren Buffett announced this month he will donate $5.47 billion to four foundations associated with his family ahead of Thanksgiving. Similarly, various students in club organizations throughout Kansas are collecting food items to give to hungry families for the holiday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spiders, beetles and one garage alligator: Largest study to date reveals wildlife sharing our indoor spaces
item.description: An international team of researchers is revealing the largest study to date detailing the wide range of insects, arachnids and other organisms that live in homes and other indoor environments across the United States and Canada. The researchers have compiled a database with more than 20,000 entries spanning more than 2,000 species found in these indoor ecosystems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep Venture: A new class of ocean exploration vehicle developed
item.description: Researchers have a new capability for exploring some of the least understood regions of the ocean. Developed by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in collaboration with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, Deep Venture is a next-generation autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) for deep-ocean research, capable of supporting a wide range of scientific missions, from shallow coastal waters to the deepest places on Earth. It can withstand extreme pressure, rated for depths of up to 11,000 meters (about 6.83 mi), or full ocean depth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anthropic researcher says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, first posed in 1859
item.description: A researcher at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm's Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new way to extract oxygen from lunar soil could support bases on the moon
item.description: Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Theory explains how fusion plasmas enter a state of improved energy confinement, solving a 40-year puzzle
item.description: Nuclear fusion promises a source of energy by combining light atomic nuclei, the same process that powers the sun. To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists must heat a gas to extreme temperatures, creating a charged state of matter called plasma. Keeping this plasma hot and stable long enough for fusion energy production is one of the main challenges facing the technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: U.K.'s nature health check doesn't stack up in wildlife's favor—but volunteers are collecting plenty of crucial data
item.description: As nature declines over time, it becomes easier to normalize an increasingly impoverished environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 logra acuerdos de inversión, pero persisten las diferencias sobre los combustibles fósiles
item.description: Aunque estaba previsto que las negociaciones de la COP31 concluyeran este 20 de noviembre, aún no se han alcanzado acuerdos definitivos sobre los combustibles fósiles. Turquía anunció acuerdos y proyectos de inversión por más de 26.000 millones de dólares. Por su parte, la financiación climática para los países en desarrollo continúa siendo uno de los principales puntos de desacuerdo. Nuestro corresponsal, Adrià Rocha, nos amplía los detalles. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Killer whales became fearsome predators long before scientists thought
item.description: Killer whales, or orcas, are among the ocean's most formidable predators, hunting everything from fish and seals to other whales. But how and when these members of the dolphin family evolved into such effective hunters has long been something of a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How desert biocrusts respond to changing snow cover
item.description: In the desert, winter snow may seem like a temporary visitor, but its effects can last long after the snow melts. By supplying water to dry ecosystems, snowfall helps sustain biological soil crusts (biocrusts), thin living layers on the soil surface that play important roles in desert ecosystems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Excitons mimic light in atom-thin material, confirming decade-old quantum prediction
item.description: Combining their skills in theory and experiment, Yale researchers have observed for the first time a type of energy-carrying composite particle move in a highly unexpected way. It's a finding that could lead to advances in quantum technologies, solar energy, LEDs and other optoelectronic technologies. The work is published in Nature Physics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Honor Awards Ceremony Recognizes Employees at Stennis Space Center
item.description: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18. Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: LaToya Dean

item.title: Researchers trace shifting pulsation modes in δ Scuti star KIC 4737720
item.description: Stars in the night sky may look calm and unchanging, but some are in fact constantly "vibrating." Just as a musical instrument can sound several notes at once, a star can pulse in several modes simultaneously. By measuring minute changes in a star's brightness, astronomers can read these stellar vibrations and, in turn, probe the physical processes at work inside it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Venus-like conditions reveal how minerals could preserve traces of ancient water
item.description: Venus is one of the most inhospitable environments in our solar system, with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead and atmospheric pressure nearly 100 times greater than Earth's. Yet its surface may preserve clues to a time when the planet looked much more like Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Male bumblebees contribute to nest care, challenging view that they only mate
item.description: For decades, researchers have assumed male bumblebees' contribution to hives consisted mainly of DNA. However, a new study finds that the males actually help incubate baby bumbles, and that with males' assistance, hives thrive. The study, published in the Royal Society Open Science journal, quantifies the beneficial effects of having male babysitters in the hive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover Collects Samples
item.description: This Nov. 16 collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. Learn more […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Misinformation perception shapes support of democracy in Australia
item.description: A new study by Adelaide University researchers has found that the more often people perceived they had encountered misinformation, the less positive their views of Australian democracy tended to be. The experience-sampling study from the School of Psychology asked 123 eligible voters to track their perceived exposure to misinformation in the lead-up to the 2025 Australian federal election and measured whether this exposure influenced their attitudes and emotions toward the election. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Low-viscosity lavas reveal a key to Mars's past
item.description: Since 2021, the Mars Perseverance rover has been roaming Jezero Crater, gathering details about the red planet's geology and hints about its past. On its journey, the rover took close-up images of the Séítah formation, a nearly 4-billion-year-old layer of rock at the base of the crater. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31 climate talks go into overtime as nations quarrel over fossil fuels
item.description: The COP31 climate conference slipped into overtime on Friday as negotiators from nearly 200 ⁠countries struggled to bridge deep divisions ⁠over fossil fuels and climate finance. Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference ⁠heaped pressure on host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, saying the meeting was on track to be the “worst COP ever” because it lacked ambition to address the worsening climate crisis. The biggest points of tension centre around whether a final deal should... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
item.description: Russia launched a Soyuz rocket with satellites to help enable drone attacks over Ukraine. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Activists protest failure of COP31 to advance on moving away from fossil fuels
item.description: Civil society groups and activists on Friday protested against UN climate talks' failure to advance ideas to move away from fossils fuels. Fuente: Africanews.
item.dc:creator: editorial@africanews.com (Rédaction Africanews)

item.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
item.description: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
item.description: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
item.description: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
item.description: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: France awaits verdict in landmark police brutality trial over Michel Zecler assault
item.description: A French prosecutor on Thursday urged a court to jail three policemen who beat up a black music producer to four to six years, in a rare case of alleged police brutality to go to criminal court. The assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, triggered renewed outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases. The prosecutor argued the case had caused "immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole," and that those on trial had "betrayed" their uniform. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Somos casi tan pobres hoy como en 2018
item.description: La economía española ni va como una moto ni como un cohete y ni siquiera es la que más crece entre los países de la Unión Europea. Leer Fuente: Expansión - Economía.
item.dc:creator: Clemente Polo

item.title: En 1986, Florida asfaltó carreteras con residuos radiactivos para ahorrar dinero. Hoy quieren volver a hacerlo
item.description: Se llama Bone Valley, está en el centro de Florida y contiene uno de los mayores depósitos conocidos de fosfato de todo Estados Unidos. La fotografía es particular, igual que encuentras grandes líneas para el transporte de roca salido de sus minas puedes alojarte en resorts gigantescos para jugar al golf sobre algunos de los yacimientos de fósiles prehistóricos más antiguos del país. Si utilizas una cámara verás, a lo lejos, enormes montañas blancas. Montañas que son un problema para los vecinos. Montañas radioactivas que ya hay quien propone enterrar bajo el asfalto. Bone Valley . Como… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Alberto de la Torre

item.title: The far right is 'missing the butt' of the GTA VI joke: It's them!
item.description: PRESS REVIEW – Friday, November 20: We look at reactions to the historic summit in Shenzhen between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Also, COP31 heads into its final stretch, but fossil fuels have vanished from the draft deal. Plus, the Guardian features a long read on "Power Slapping". Finally, we look at a different kind of hobby: "Grand Theft Auto VI" is finally out. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Emily BOYLE

item.title: Galactic shock: Discovery challenges our understanding of the Milky Way's structure
item.description: A University of Sydney Ph.D. student has uncovered evidence that the Milky Way is unusual in terms of where its new stars are born compared with nearby galaxies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A two-layer flat lens uses nanoscale pillars to guard against unwanted reflections
item.description: Researchers in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) have engineered an advancement in metasurface design and processing that now includes a built-in, intentionally designed antireflective coating—a potentially critical step toward greatly expanding the incorporation of metasurfaces into practical devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
item.description: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: UN climate talks enter crunch time with no deal in sight
item.description: The U.N.'s COP31 climate talks enter their endgame Friday, with countries sharply divided over a draft deal lacking any mention of planet-heating fossil fuels, threatening to push the negotiations into overtime. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fiona the hippo dies after failed effort to remove swallowed hat
item.description: World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nature's multilayered defenses against crop pests and viruses revealed
item.description: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, in collaboration with Syngenta and Keele University, have discovered how a commercial barley hybrid uses three complementary natural defenses to protect itself against aphids and the damaging viruses they spread. The findings could help breeders develop crops with stronger natural protection against pests and diseases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Una estrella de Andrómeda se zampó a su vecina. Detectarlo fue como buscar el agua de un cubo en el mar
item.description: Cuando las estrellas envejecen , su envoltura se hincha hasta el punto de engullir buena parte de la materia que les rodea. Por ejemplo, si una gigante roja tiene una estrella compañera, podría devorarla por el camino. Es algo que se cree desde hace mucho tiempo. Sin embargo, los científicos no han logrado captar este proceso de principio a fin. Al menos hasta ahora. Y es que, recientemente, un equipo de astrónomos dirigido desde la Universidad de Columbia acaba de describir el que podría ser el primer evento de este tipo detectado por los telescopios. Es cierto que no se puede afirmar con… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
item.description: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 20 – V-G-R
item.description: APODScienceAPODAPOD: 2026 November…Today’s APODArchiveSubmissionsIndexSearchCalendarRSSEducationAboutDiscuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. V-G-R Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
item.description: Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
item.description: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors. At the Institute of Theoretical and Computational Physics at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), a team led by Christopher Albert has developed the "computor" learning platform for this purpose. The system is already being used in teaching and is… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
item.description: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How nature-based solutions are failing informal settlements
item.description: New research from UCT says nature-based solutions for climate adaptation must move beyond participation to power-sharing partnerships that recognize lived experiences and relationships with nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extreme weather poses growing risks to global oil and natural gas shipping, new IEA report finds
item.description: Extreme weather events are posing significant risks to international oil and natural gas shipping, with the potential to damage critical infrastructure, disrupt major trade routes and threaten energy security, according to a new IEA report. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
item.description: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
item.description: Today's artificial intelligence models can predict whether someone with a genetic change will develop a disease, but cannot answer two critical questions: Why did the disease occur, and how do we design a treatment? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
item.description: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
item.description: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
item.description: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best
item.description: A major review involving more than 30,000 people found that three antidepressants, including Lexapro and Cymbalta, may be more effective than Prozac at maintaining improvements in depression symptoms. However, limitations in the research and a lack of truly long-term data mean scientists still cannot say which antidepressant is best. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
item.description: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study: The last bird to go extinct in NZ has lessons for saving other species
item.description: The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NEPTUNE poised to replace Navy's global weather model, improving forecasts over open ocean
item.description: The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory-developed Navy Environmental Prediction sysTem Utilizing a Nonhydrostatic Engine, known as NEPTUNE, is poised to become an operational Navy weather prediction capability, providing improved environmental forecasts to support naval operations around the globe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI companions could help reduce loneliness, study finds
item.description: AI companions could help reduce loneliness by creating a greater sense of belonging and improving self-esteem, according to new research from Durham University Business School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Making hydrogen peroxide without using precious metals
item.description: Hydrogen peroxide is used in many industrial processes, with several million tons of it being manufactured worldwide every year. Whereas the standard production method requires rare precious metals, chemists from Rutgers University–Newark in the US and the University of Bonn have now described an alternative technique that does away with these metals, making it potentially cheaper and more sustainable. Their findings have now been published in the journal Nature Communications. In the following interview, the authors describe the technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
item.description: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Mercury-bound X-ray telescope delivers first images after eight years in space
item.description: The first data from a U.K.-built instrument heading to Mercury have provided observations of one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky from aboard the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo spacecraft in the inner solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
item.description: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Britain should treat healthy seas as essential infrastructure, say scientists
item.description: Researchers are calling for lasting investment in healthy seas to support food security, protect coastlines and strengthen economic resilience. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
item.description: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start
item.description: If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
item.description: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dual-purpose polymer dots could combine bioimaging and light-triggered cell death in one material
item.description: A research team led by professor Youhei Takeda at the University of Osaka, in collaboration with professor Zachary M. Hudson at the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has developed a polymer material that combines fluorescent cell imaging with the potential to kill cancer cells when activated by light. The material could offer a simpler approach to developing "nanotheranostic" technologies, which bring disease imaging and treatment together in a single platform. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
item.description: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
item.description: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ESA's Hera probe uses 'superhuman' vision to inspect NASA's asteroid crash site
item.description: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour (13,700 miles per hour). However, we still don't know just how much of a success it actually was—DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
item.description: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches one light-day milestone
item.description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years, hit a milestone distance of one light-day away from Earth on Wednesday. Already the most distant man-made object in the universe, the spacecraft is now about 26 billion kilometers (16 billion miles) away, according to the US space agency. That is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: The snake with a built-in egg peeler
item.description: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a tiny chemical mark on a protein can be placed to double gene activity
item.description: Tiny chemical marks on histones—the proteins that package our DNA—can profoundly influence gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence. One such mark, known as histone acetylation, plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and is frequently disrupted in diseases such as cancer. Researchers, however, wondered how the enzymes responsible for adding these marks know exactly where to place them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
item.description: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
item.description: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ethiopian volcano's mysterious methane outburst may have a culprit—magma that never erupted
item.description: Experts were puzzled when satellite observations showed a volcano in Ethiopia emitting huge quantities of methane despite not erupting, but a team of researchers led by the University of Bristol believe they have discovered why this happened—and their findings could have implications for historical climate change research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ahead of Giving Tuesday, study finds charitable giving often misses communities with greatest need
item.description: As Giving Tuesday approaches, a recent study led by a University of Massachusetts Amherst public policy researcher finds that communities with greater economic disadvantage typically see less private charitable giving—despite having greater needs in many cases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Remote jobs diminish hiring bias against mothers
item.description: The "motherhood penalty"—a workplace bias that assumes mothers are less committed to their careers, resulting in fewer opportunities, lower pay and slower advancement—could be reduced by shifting jobs from in-person to remote, according to new research by Claire Daviss, assistant professor of organizational behavior at the ILR School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
item.description: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Improving hydrogen production from water can support abundant global crops
item.description: Water, at least in its purest form, contains hydrogen and oxygen. In 1800, scientists first used electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. Today, this process, known as water electrolysis, is widely used to produce hydrogen for industrial purposes, including manufacturing ammonia for agricultural fertilizers that sustain global food production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-rays reveal fleeting intermediate step as iron-containing molecule responds to light
item.description: A research team has traced how a molecule rearranges its electrons when excited by light. The findings, published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition, help clarify a long-standing question and open new possibilities for studying chemistry in motion, such as bonds breaking or forming—fundamental steps in reactions involving catalysts and biological molecules. The collaboration included Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB), the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, Switzerland, and European XFEL. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research explains how far people will go for a day at the park
item.description: A park two miles (3.2 kilometers) from home might seem close enough for a Saturday outing. In metropolitan Detroit, though, park visits had already fallen to about half their modeled peak by that distance. In metropolitan Minneapolis, the same drop took nearly five miles (8 kilometers). And in the New York metropolitan area, with its extensive transit network, visitation fell by half at about 2.3 miles (3.7 kilometers). A park's reach, it turns out, depends a great deal on where it is. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Modified genetic method allows researchers to quantify roots growing underground
item.description: Plant scientists know that what grows above the soil doesn't offer enough information to understand an entire plant community. Different species contribute differently to belowground biomass, and those differences matter for soil health and ecosystem functioning. However, digging up roots to separate and identify them by species, especially when many plants are growing together underground, can be difficult and time-consuming, according to a team of researchers in the College of Agricultural Sciences at Penn State. Fuente: Phys.org.
